title: The Last Leaf
author: O. Henry (retold)
summary: 肺炎にかかった若い画家ジョンジーは、窓の外のツタの葉が全部落ちたら自分も死ぬと思い込みます。O・ヘンリー「最後の一葉」。

source.note: Retold in simpler English from O. Henry’s “The Last Leaf” (1907, public domain).

paragraphs: In a small district west of Washington Square in New York, the streets have gone crazy and broken themselves into little strips called “places.” These places make strange angles and curves. One street even crosses itself once or twice. Artists discovered this old neighborhood, Greenwich Village, because the rents were cheap and the old houses had north-facing windows with good light for painting.

At the top of a three-story brick building, Sue and Johnsy had their studio. Johnsy was short for Joanna. One was from Maine, the other from California. They had met at a cheap restaurant on Eighth Street and discovered that they liked the same art, the same food and the same kind of sleeves. So they decided to share a studio.

That was in May. In November, a cold, invisible stranger, whom the doctors called Pneumonia, came to the colony. He walked boldly across the east side, touching people here and there with his icy fingers, and hitting dozens of victims. But he moved more slowly through the narrow, mossy streets of the Village. Unfortunately, he found Johnsy. She lay, hardly moving, on her painted iron bed, looking through the small window at the blank brick wall of the house next door.

One morning, the busy doctor took Sue into the hallway. “She has one chance in ten,” he said, shaking down the thermometer. “And that chance is for her to want to live. When people decide they are going to die, medicine cannot do much. Your little lady has made up her mind that she is not going to get well. Is there anything on her mind?”
“She wanted to paint the Bay of Naples someday,” said Sue.
“Paint? Nonsense! Is there anything worth thinking about twice? A man, for example?”
“A man?” said Sue. “Is a man worth... no, doctor, there is nothing of the kind.”
“Well,” said the doctor, “I will do everything science can do. But if you can make her ask one question about the new winter fashions, her chance will be one in five instead of one in ten.”

After the doctor left, Sue went into her workroom and cried until her napkin was wet. Then she walked into Johnsy’s room with her drawing board, whistling cheerfully. She needed to work; she was drawing pictures for a magazine story.

Johnsy lay with her face toward the window. Sue stopped whistling, thinking she was asleep. Then she heard a low voice, repeated several times. Johnsy was looking out of the window and counting backward.
“Twelve,” she said, and a little later, “Eleven,” and then “Ten,” and “Nine,” and then “Eight” and “Seven,” almost together.

Sue looked out of the window. What was there to count? There was only a bare, empty yard and the blank wall of the brick house twenty feet away. An old, old ivy vine, twisted and rotting at the roots, climbed halfway up the wall. The cold breath of autumn had blown away its leaves, and its bare branches clung to the bricks.
“What is it, dear?” asked Sue.

“Six,” said Johnsy, almost in a whisper. “They’re falling faster now. Three days ago there were almost a hundred. It made my head hurt to count them. But now it’s easy. There goes another one. There are only five left now.”
“Five what, dear? Tell your Sudie.”
“Leaves. On the ivy vine. When the last one falls, I must go too. I’ve known that for three days. Didn’t the doctor tell you?”

“Oh, I never heard such nonsense!” said Sue. “What do old ivy leaves have to do with your getting well? And you used to love that vine so much, you naughty girl. Don’t be silly. The doctor told me this morning that your chances of getting well soon were, let me see, he said ten to one! Now try to eat some soup, and let me finish my drawing so I can sell it and buy wine for my sick child and pork chops for my greedy self.”

“You don’t need to buy any more wine,” said Johnsy, still looking out of the window. “There goes another. No, I don’t want any soup. That leaves just four. I want to see the last one fall before it gets dark. Then I’ll go too.”

Sue made her promise to close her eyes and not look out of the window until she had finished her work. “I need the light,” she said, “or I would pull the curtain down.” Then she went downstairs to find Behrman, who lived on the ground floor.

Old Behrman was a painter over sixty years old, with a long gray beard. He was a failure in art. For forty years he had been planning to paint a masterpiece, but he had never even begun it. He earned a little money by posing as a model for the young artists in the colony, and he drank too much gin. He was a fierce little old man who laughed at softness in others, but he thought of himself as the special protector of the two young women upstairs.

Sue found him in his dark, gin-smelling room. In one corner stood an empty canvas on an easel. It had been waiting twenty-five years for the first line of the masterpiece. She told him about Johnsy’s idea, and how she feared that Johnsy, as light and weak as a leaf herself, would float away when her hold on the world grew weaker.

Old Behrman, with his red eyes watering, shouted his contempt for such silly ideas. “What!” he cried. “Are there people in the world so foolish that they die because leaves fall off a stupid vine? I have never heard of such a thing. Why do you let such nonsense come into her head? Ah, poor little Miss Johnsy.” But he went upstairs with Sue.

Johnsy was asleep. Sue pulled the curtain down, and she and Behrman went into the other room. They looked out of the window at the ivy vine with fear. Then they looked at each other for a moment without speaking. A cold rain was falling, mixed with snow.
When Johnsy woke up the next morning, she said in a weak voice, “Pull up the curtain. I want to see.”
Sue pulled it up, tired and unhappy.

But after the beating rain and fierce wind that had lasted all night, there was still one ivy leaf against the brick wall. It was the last on the vine. It was still dark green near its stem, but its edges were yellow with age, and it hung bravely from a branch about twenty feet above the ground.
“It is the last one,” said Johnsy. “I thought it would surely fall during the night. I heard the wind. It will fall today, and I shall die at the same time.”
The day passed, and even in the evening light they could see the lonely leaf hanging on the wall. When night came, the north wind blew again, and rain beat against the windows.
When it was light enough, Johnsy again asked for the curtain to be raised. The ivy leaf was still there.
Johnsy lay for a long time looking at it. Then she called to Sue, who was cooking chicken soup over the gas stove.

“I’ve been a bad girl, Sudie,” said Johnsy. “Something has made that last leaf stay there to show me how wicked I was. It is a sin to want to die. You may bring me a little soup now, and some milk with a little wine in it, and... no; bring me a hand mirror first, and then put some pillows around me, and I will sit up and watch you cook.” An hour later she said: “Sudie, someday I hope to paint the Bay of Naples.”

The doctor came in the afternoon. As he was leaving, he took Sue’s thin, shaking hand. “Even chances,” he said. “With good nursing, you’ll win. And now I must see another case downstairs. Behrman, his name is. Some kind of artist, I believe. Pneumonia too. He is an old, weak man, and the attack is severe. There is no hope for him, but he goes to the hospital today to make him more comfortable.”
The next day the doctor said to Sue: “She’s out of danger. You’ve won. Nutrition and care now, that’s all.”
That afternoon Sue came to the bed where Johnsy lay, happily knitting a very blue and very useless wool scarf, and put one arm around her, pillows and all.

“I have something to tell you, little white mouse,” she said. “Mr. Behrman died of pneumonia today in the hospital. He was sick only two days. The janitor found him on the morning of the first day in his room downstairs, helpless with pain. His shoes and clothes were completely wet and icy cold. They couldn’t imagine where he had been on such a terrible night. And then they found a lantern, still lit, and a ladder that had been moved from its place, and some scattered brushes, and a palette with green and yellow colors mixed on it, and... look out of the window, dear, at the last ivy leaf on the wall. Didn’t you wonder why it never moved when the wind blew? Ah, darling, it’s Behrman’s masterpiece. He painted it there the night that the last leaf fell.”
